title: How much are the tomatoes?
goal: Shop at the market with numbers, units and prices — and untangle the only real complication in Bulgarian numbers: a special counting form for masculine nouns, and yet another form just for men.
bekal: count from zero to a thousand
ask prices with **колко струва** and **колко струват**
use **два** and **две** according to the noun
use the masculine counting form: *два лева*, *три хляба*
pay, get your change, and close the deal politely

dialogs.title: Диалог — At the Женски пазар market
dialogs.intro: Ani is shopping at Sofia's biggest open-air market. Notice that nouns after numbers end in **-а**, which isn't the ordinary plural — that's the masculine counting form.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Good afternoon! How much are the tomatoes?

lines.speaker: Продавач:
lines.id: Three leva a kilo. They're really nice.
lines.literal: three — leva — kilo-the. very — are — nice.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: One kilo, please. And two cucumbers.
lines.literal: give-(formal) — to-me — one — kilogram, please. and — two — cucumbers.

lines.speaker: Продавач:
lines.id: Twelve leva a kilo. Would you like half a kilo?
lines.literal: twelve — leva — kilo-the. want-you-(formal) — (question) — half — kilo?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes, please. And a loaf of bread.

lines.speaker: Продавач:
lines.id: That's twelve leva fifty stotinki altogether.
lines.literal: everything — is — twelve — leva — and — fifty — stotinki.

lines.speaker: Продавач:
lines.id: Here's your change — seven leva fifty. Thank you!
lines.literal: here-is — change-the — seven — leva — and — fifty. thank-you!

notes: ⚠️ **Masculine nouns after a number take a special form, not the ordinary plural.** The plural of *лев* is *левове*, but after a number it becomes **лева**: *два лева, пет лева, сто лева*. Likewise *хляб* → plural *хлябове*, but *два хляба*. This is called the **бройна форма** — the counting form — and it exists only for masculine nouns that aren't people.
**Дайте ми literally means "give to me".** The *ми* is the short form "to me" you've already seen in *Приятно ми е*. To a friend it's *Дай ми*.

**Заповядайте is the most versatile word in Bulgaria.** It's used when handing something over ("here you are"), inviting someone in ("come in"), offering a seat, and when a waiter greets you ("yes, what would you like?"). The informal form is *Заповядай*. If you learn only ten words from this unit, include this one.
**Килото means "per kilo", with the article.** It's like English "three leva **the** kilo": *три лева килото*. The same pattern works for *бройката* (each, per piece) and *литърът* (per liter).

**Bulgarian money: лев, plural левове, counting form лева.** One lev is a hundred **стотинки** (from *сто*, a hundred). In conversation people often give a price without the unit at all: *дванайсет и петдесет* clearly means 12.50 lv.

**Струва for one thing, струват for several.** *Колко струва хлябът?* (How much is the bread?) and *Колко струват доматите?* (How much are the tomatoes?). Just like English "is" vs "are" — and here too the agreement is required.
**Друго? is how a seller asks "anything else?"** The closing answer: *Не, благодаря. Това е всичко.* (No, thanks. That's all.)
**Аз благодаря — "thank YOU".** A warm and very common closing line; putting *аз* in front shifts the emphasis onto you. The seller will remember you.

grammars.title: Numbers 1–20 and beyond
body: Numbers 1 to 10 have to be memorized; the rest are built from the same bricks.
after: Numbers 11 to 19 all follow the pattern **number + найсет**, which comes from *на десет* — "on ten", much like English "-teen". If you can say 1 to 10, you can practically say 1 to 20.
Compound numbers are joined with **и** before the last part: *двайсет и едно* (21), *сто двайсет и пет* (125), *хиляда деветстотин деветдесет и девет* (1999).

grammars.title: Един, два, and the masculine counting form
body: Only one and two follow gender. Three and up never change. What changes instead is **the noun** — and only if it's masculine.
after: The last row is an oddity to learn separately: **for men, the number itself changes** — *двама, трима, четирима, петима, шестима*. These forms are used only for male people or mixed groups. For women alone, the ordinary numbers are used: *две жени*.
⚠️ The most common trap: saying *два лева* correctly and then *два мъжа* — which is wrong twice over. The right form is **двама мъже**.
The shortest way to remember it: **masculine thing → the noun changes; male people → the number changes.**

sections.title: Shopping phrases that cover the whole transaction

head: Български
Say it
English
rows: Може ли да платя с карта?
MO-zheh lee da pla-TYA s KAR-ta

blocks.text: ⚠️ You'll usually hear the last line from the seller, not say it yourself. At open markets, paying for something that costs three leva with a fifty is often gently refused. Keep small change — in Bulgaria it's worth more than its face value.

At the market, small quantities are often given with no unit at all: *два домата* (two tomatoes), *три краставици* (three cucumbers). The seller will understand. Just don't forget the masculine counting form — *домат* is masculine, so **два домата**, not *два домати*.

blocks.title: Кисело мляко — the yogurt that carries the country's name
items: If you shop in Bulgaria, one product will always be in a local's basket: **кисело мляко** (*KEE-seh-lo MLYA-ko*), literally "sour milk", meaning yogurt. The bacterium that makes it, *Lactobacillus bulgaricus*, is named after this country because it was discovered here in 1905 by a Bulgarian student.

Yogurt isn't a side dish in Bulgaria; it's a staple. It becomes the cold soup *таратор* in summer, a sauce, the salty drink *айрян*, and it's eaten plain with honey. If you ask *Кое кисело мляко е най-хубавото?* (Which yogurt is the best?), get ready for a long and serious conversation.
